story: Bigger than whatever you're picturing. Now go bigger.

panels.name: Compared with a typical large mammal
rows: Milk a calf drinks per day

hints: Check the weight. Those are tonnes, not kilograms.
A heart as heavy as a very large person, fuelled by tonnes of tiny krill.
why: About 30 m long, up to about 190 tonnes, a heart of about 180 kg, about 4 tonnes of krill a day and calls up to about 188 decibels. It's the blue whale, the heaviest animal known to have lived. Picked the fin whale? Second place, and still enormous.
pearl: Scientists can age whales by counting layers in their earwax, and the oldest blue whale aged that way was about 110.

story: Snowy, salty and home to a heart-stopping medical first.

panels.name: Compared with a typical big US city

hints: An Olympic host, high in the snowy mountains of the western US.
Its name comes from the big, briny lake next door. A famous artificial heart went in here too.
why: About 1,320 m up, about 150 cm of snow a year, about 200,000 people, the 2002 Winter Olympics and the University of Utah's 1982 artificial heart implant. It's Salt Lake City. Denver is the classic guess, but it has never hosted the Winter Games.
pearl: The first patient to receive a permanent artificial heart got it here in December 1982 and lived for 112 days, with the pump's compressor rolling along beside him.

story: Long. Longer than that. And the famous space claim is a myth.

panels.name: Compared with a typical defensive wall
rows: Visible from the Moon with the naked eye

hints: Check the total length. That's more than a very long way.
Built, added to and repaired over more than two thousand years.
key: Visible from the Moon with the naked eye
why: About 21,200 km of walls and trenches, built on and off for about 2,300 years, up to about 8 m high in well-kept stretches. It's the Great Wall of China. Hadrian's Wall is lovely, but it's about 120 km. No, it can't be seen from the Moon.
pearl: NASA says it's only barely visible from low Earth orbit, and only under nearly perfect conditions, because it's narrow and made of local materials that blend into the landscape.

story: Happy International Cheetah Day. This one isn't a cheetah, but it can keep going for far longer.

panels.name: Compared with a typical North American grazer
rows: Horns' outer sheath shed each year

hints: A runner with staying power, and it lives in North America. Africa is out.
It looks like an antelope, but it's alone in its family, and it sheds its horn covers every year.
Horns' outer sheath shed each year
why: Up to about 88 km/h, about 56 km/h over 6.5 km, huge eyes with about 320 degrees of vision, and the last living species in its family. It's the pronghorn. It looks like an antelope and is often called one, but its closest living relatives are giraffes and okapis.
pearl: Some biologists think it's so fast because its ancestors had to outrun an extinct American cheetah-like cat. Today nothing in North America can catch it, so it's a bit overqualified.

story: Small, steep and very, very green.
hints: A country that held out on TV until 1999.
More forest than almost anywhere, enough to soak up more carbon than it emits.
why: About 0.8 million people, a top peak of about 7,570 m, about 71% forest, no TV until 1999, about US$100 a day for most visitors, and forests that absorb more greenhouse gas than it emits. It's Bhutan, the Himalayan kingdom famous for Gross National Happiness. Nepal is the mix-up, but Nepal has far more people and far less forest.
pearl: Its tallest peak, Gangkhar Puensum, is often called the highest unclimbed mountain in the world.

story: The biggest of its kind, with something no other in its class has.

panels.name: Compared with a typical moon
rows: Size next to the planet Mercury

hints: Size next to the planet Mercury
The only moon known to make its own magnetic field.
key: Size next to the planet Mercury
why: About 5,270 km across, bigger than Mercury, gravity about 0.15 of Earth's, and the only moon known to generate its own magnetic field. It's Ganymede, Jupiter's largest moon and the largest in the solar system. Titan comes close at about 5,150 km but has no magnetic field of its own.
pearl: ESA's JUICE spacecraft is due to go into orbit around Ganymede in the 2030s, which would make it the first moon other than our own to be orbited by a spacecraft.

story: Flat, busy and partly dry on purpose. An airline pioneer too.
hints: About a quarter of the country is lower than the sea.
The world's oldest airline still using its original name, and Rotterdam's the port.
why: About 18 million people, about 26% of land below sea level, about 540 people per km², an airline from 1919, the world's second-biggest food exporter by value, and the busiest port in Europe in Rotterdam. It's the Netherlands. Belgium is next door but has much less land below the waves.
pearl: KLM was founded on 7 October 1919 and is the oldest operating airline still flying under its original name.

story: Dresses formally. Parents in the worst weather on Earth.
hints: Flightless, and a seriously deep diver.
Dads go about four months without food, in about −40 °C, while looking after an egg.
why: Up to about 45 kg, dives to about 564 m for about 22 minutes, fathers fasting for about 120 days, and air temperatures down to about −40 °C. It's the emperor penguin. The king penguin looks similar, but it's smaller and doesn't breed through the Antarctic winter.
pearl: Males balance the egg on their feet for about 65 to 75 days while the females are off feeding at sea. They can lose about 20 kg over the long fast.

story: Big, beautiful and with a foot in two places at once.

panels.name: Compared with a typical big city
rows: Rail and road tunnels between continents

hints: How many continents do most cities need? This one has two.
You can commute under the strait between Europe and Asia. It lost its capital status, and at least one old name.
Rail and road tunnels between continents
key: Rail and road tunnels between continents
why: About 15.8 million people, on both Europe and Asia, about 18% of its country's population, and two tunnels under the Bosphorus. It's Istanbul. Ankara is Turkey's capital, but it's nowhere near as big and sits on only one continent.
pearl: Earlier names include Byzantium and Constantinople. Two-thirds of its people live on the European side, with many commuting across the strait, and a catchy 1953 song reminded everyone that it's Istanbul, not Constantinople.

story: Old. Heavy. Pointy. And its record lasted a very long time.

panels.name: Compared with a typical ancient tomb
rows: Years as the world's tallest structure
Still standing from the original Seven Wonders

hints: Only one Wonder from the ancient list is still standing.
Still standing from the original Seven Wonders
It was the tallest thing humans had built for about 3,700 years.
Years as the world's tallest structure
key: Still standing from the original Seven Wonders
Years as the world's tallest structure
why: About 147 m tall when finished, about 2.3 million blocks, about 6 million tonnes, the tallest structure for over 3,700 years, and the only ancient Wonder largely intact. It's the Great Pyramid of Giza, built for the pharaoh Khufu. Khafre's pyramid next door looks taller from some angles, but it isn't.
pearl: Today it stands about 138.5 m tall, as it lost its outer casing and top over time. It's estimated to have been built in around 26 years, about 4,600 years ago.

story: Happy International Mountain Day. It treats the world's highest range as a shortcut.
hints: An ordinary-sized goose with one very unusual commute.
Its blood is specially tuned to thin air, and the name describes the stripes on its head.
why: Tracked at about 7,290 m, about 2.5 kg, and able to cross the Himalaya in as little as about 7 hours from near sea level, thanks to haemoglobin that grips oxygen harder. It's the bar-headed goose. Rüppell's vulture flies higher still, but it's far bigger, and it's a vulture.
pearl: Those stories of geese flying over Everest at 8,000 m or more are probably tall tales. Tracking shows that they usually prefer the high passes, which is smart for a goose.

story: Happy Health For All Day. This country swapped its army for other priorities.

panels.name: Compared with a typical country
rows: Oceans or seas it has coasts on

hints: A small Central American country with no army.
Nearly all its power comes from renewables, and it has coasts on the Caribbean and the Pacific.
Oceans or seas it has coasts on
why: About 5.2 million people, about 51,000 km², no army since 1948, about 95% renewable electricity, coasts on the Caribbean and Pacific, and a social health insurer that began in 1941. It's Costa Rica. Panama also has no regular army, but only since 1990.
pearl: 'Pura vida', literally 'pure life', works as hello, goodbye and 'how are you?' all at once.

story: Similar to Earth in size. Similar to nothing in comfort.
hints: Almost exactly Earth's size, but 464 °C at the surface.
The hottest planet of all, and it spins the 'wrong' way, very slowly.
why: Almost Earth's size and gravity, but about 464 °C, about 93 times Earth's air pressure, a spin that takes about 243 Earth days and runs backwards, and no moons. It's Venus. Mercury is closer to the Sun, but Venus's thick carbon dioxide atmosphere (about 96.5%) makes it hotter.
pearl: A Venus year is about 225 Earth days, so one full spin takes longer than a whole trip around the Sun.

story: Huge, colourful and the home of far more than one language.

panels.name: Compared with a typical country
rows: Most native Spanish speakers on Earth

hints: Spain started the language, but which country has the most native speakers?
Most native Spanish speakers on Earth
key: Most native Spanish speakers on Earth
why: About 134 million people, about 2 million km², 68 recognised Indigenous languages, about 29% of the world's avocados, and more native Spanish speakers than anywhere else. It's Mexico. Spain gave the language its name, but it has far fewer speakers.
pearl: Maize, tomatoes and beans were all domesticated here. Take a moment before your next taco to thank the ancient farmers.

story: White fur, black skin, and a very cold office.
hints: A bear that swims 154 km? It must have a good reason.
Its name in Latin is 'sea bear', and its fur has no pigment at all.
why: Males up to about 800 kg, swims averaging about 154 km in one study, fur with no pigment over black skin, and the Latin name Ursus maritimus, sea bear. It's the polar bear, the biggest living land carnivore. Kodiak bears come close in size, but they stay brown and on land.
pearl: Its fur only looks white, as it scatters light, and its hairs are transparent. Its skin, nose and lips are black.

story: Happy Beethoven's birthday. A city that takes its music, and its dancing, very seriously.

panels.name: Compared with a typical European capital
rows: Flats built by the city, 1925 to 1934

hints: Beethoven came here, and so did all those dancers.
A capital on the Danube with hundreds of formal balls.
key: Flats built by the city, 1925 to 1934
why: About 2 million people, about 450 balls a year in a season from 11 November to Shrove Tuesday, over 60,000 city-built flats between 1925 and 1934, and Beethoven among the composers who moved here. It's Vienna. Salzburg was Mozart's birthplace, but Beethoven's address and the balls are in Vienna.
pearl: The Vienna Chamber of Commerce estimated over 500,000 people attended balls in the 2018 season, spending about €139 million. Those shoes aren't going to dance themselves.

story: Happy First Flight Day. This building's pointy top was meant for airships.

panels.name: Compared with a typical 1930s office tower
rows: Years as the world's tallest building

hints: An airship dock at the top of a skyscraper. What could go wrong?
Started in 1930 and open by 1931, it then held the title of world's tallest for decades. A very famous gorilla climbed it too.
Years as the world's tallest building
why: About 443 m to the tip, 102 floors, built in about 13.5 months, the world's tallest for about 39 years, 73 lifts and a mast designed for docking airships. It's New York's Empire State Building. The Chrysler Building is the near neighbour, but it was only the tallest for about a year.
pearl: The airship plan was dropped because high winds would have made docking impossible. Imagine leaving an airship by gangplank, 102 floors up.

story: Happy International Migrants Day. The champion traveller weighs about as much as a bar of soap.

panels.name: Compared with a typical migratory bird

hints: Small bird, enormous mileage. Check the migration per year.
It sees two summers a year by flying from one end of the planet to the other.
why: About 70,900 km a year, about 100 g, two summers a year, about 2.4 million km in a lifetime and up to about 31 years. It's the Arctic tern, flying between the Arctic and Antarctic. The common tern's lovely but goes nowhere near this far. And the godwit holds a different record, for non-stop flights.
pearl: It's thought to see more daylight than any other creature, and its lifetime mileage is about three return trips to the Moon.

story: An ark for animals found almost nowhere else.

panels.name: Compared with a typical country
rows: World rank among islands by size

hints: The lemur number is the giveaway, and there's not a monkey in sight.
A huge island, off the coast of Africa.
World rank among islands by size
why: About 32 million people, the world's fourth-largest island, over 90% of its wildlife found nowhere else, about 103 kinds of lemur, no native monkeys and six of the world's nine baobab species. It's Madagascar. Mozambique is the nearest mainland neighbour, but it has no lemurs.
pearl: Lemurs evolved here without monkeys to compete with. Yes, the animated film got that bit right.

story: Small, shiny and constantly spraying.

panels.name: Compared with a typical moon
rows: Feeds one of its planet's rings

hints: One of the shiniest objects in the solar system, even though it's tiny.
Its jets of salty water supply most of the material in a ring around Saturn.
Feeds one of its planet's rings
key: Feeds one of its planet's rings
why: About 500 km across, an albedo of about 1.38, about −198 °C on average, jets of salty water from cracks near its south pole, and most of the material in Saturn's E ring. It's Enceladus. Europa may have its own ocean, but it's many times larger.
pearl: Its south-pole cracks are nicknamed tiger stripes, and the jets show a salty ocean under the ice.

story: Happy World Meditation Day. Breathe in. So will about a billion and a half others.
hints: The most populous country on Earth. Not who you may have thought.
why: About 1.48 billion people, the world's biggest population, about 3.3 million km², 22 languages recognised in its constitution, 45 UNESCO sites and the home of yoga. It's India. China was top for a long time, but India now has the most people.
pearl: Hindi and English are the official languages of the central government, and the 22 languages on the constitution's list are only some of those spoken.

story: Happy Ramanujan's birthday. A mathematician would enjoy counting this one's body parts.

panels.name: Compared with a typical sea creature
rows: Share of neurons in the arms

hints: Three hearts and eight arms. That's a lot to keep track of.
Most of its brainpower lives in its arms.
Share of neurons in the arms
why: Three hearts, eight arms, over 500 million neurons (about as many as a dog) with about two-thirds in the arms, blue blood and a short life of up to about four years. It's the octopus. Squid have tentacles too, but they count two more limbs.
pearl: Female giant Pacific octopuses guard their eggs for about five months, up to 180,000 of them, and die after they hatch. Adult octopuses, even big ones, can squeeze through a gap of a little over 2.5 cm.

story: Happy Twin Transplant Day. Old, clever and home to a twin-powered medical first.

panels.name: Compared with a typical big US city

hints: Check the dates: it has been around since 1630, and had the first subway in the US.
Over 50 colleges nearby, and a kidney transplant that made history.
why: About 670,000 people, a town since 1630, the first US subway in 1897, a public school from 1635, over 50 colleges nearby, and the first successful kidney transplant. It's Boston. Philadelphia is similarly historic, but those two 'firsts' belong here.
pearl: On 23 December 1954 at Brigham Hospital, Ronald Herrick gave a kidney to his identical twin, Richard. Identical twins share tissue types, which meant far less risk of rejection.

story: A white marble love letter, on a very large scale.
hints: An emperor built this for his late wife.
White marble with 28 kinds of inlaid gemstone, and about 5 million visitors a year.
why: About 73 m tall, over 20,000 workers, about 21 years for the full complex, 28 kinds of stone inlaid in marble, about 5 million visitors a year, built by Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. It's the Taj Mahal in Agra. Humayun's Tomb inspired it, but it's built mainly of red sandstone and has far fewer visitors.
pearl: Its four minarets were set slightly outward so that, if they ever fell, they'd fall away from the tomb. Elephants and oxen helped haul materials up a 15 km ramp.

story: Merry Christmas. Who else would be on today's card?

panels.name: Compared with a typical deer
rows: Still has antlers in late December
Star of a 1939 department store booklet

hints: Antlers on the females. So who's really pulling the sleigh?
Still has antlers in late December
An extra-red nose, and a 1939 booklet made one famous.
Star of a 1939 department store booklet
key: Star of a 1939 department store booklet
why: Up to about 4,900 km a year on the move, one of the longest land migrations, antlers on females as well as males, and noses packed with tiny blood vessels. It's the reindeer. Moose would look great in tinsel, but they're not pulling anything tonight.
pearl: Males usually drop their antlers in early winter, so Santa's antlered team was probably female. Merry Christmas, and a nod to Isaac Newton, born on Christmas Day 1642. What goes up, must come down, except possibly a sleigh.

story: Mountainous, landlocked and very well connected.
hints: No coast, plenty of Alps. This narrows things down a bit, but not all the way.
Eight neighbours is a lot. Switzerland has fewer.
why: About 9.2 million people, about 84,000 km², about 62% of the land in the Eastern Alps, eight neighbours, about 47% forest and no coast. It's Austria. Switzerland is the mix-up, as it's also alpine and landlocked, but it has fewer neighbours.
pearl: About 63% of Austria's electricity supply comes from renewable sources.

story: Old, dark and battered. It stays out of the action.

panels.name: Compared with a typical moon
rows: Among the most cratered of all

hints: It's nearly Mercury-sized, and its surface shows old impacts.
Third biggest of all moons, and far out from the radiation of Jupiter.
why: About 4,820 km across, about 16.7 days per orbit, the third-largest moon in the solar system, and a very ancient, heavily cratered surface. It's Callisto, the outermost big moon of Jupiter. Ganymede's bigger still, with a magnetic field, and Titan's the second-biggest of all.
pearl: Callisto is barely smaller than Mercury, but it only has about a third of Mercury's mass. Being so far out, it gets a much lower radiation dose than Jupiter's inner moons.

story: Happy Stan Lee's birthday. A leap like a superhero, and it rarely needs a drink.
hints: Which antelope is South Africa's national animal? You might have seen one on rugby jerseys.
A 2 m bounce and a very long gap between drinks.
why: Top speed about 88 km/h, bounces up to about 2 m, about 35 kg, can go years without drinking thanks to juicy plants, and South Africa's national animal. It's the springbok. Pronghorns match the speed, but they live in North America.
pearl: That stiff-legged bounce is called pronking. Millions of them once migrated in herds hundreds of kilometres long, a phenomenon called trekbokking.

story: Black, white and permanently snacking.

panels.name: Compared with a typical bear
rows: Mother weighs this much more than her newborn

hints: A bear on an almost entirely bamboo diet.
A false thumb helps it grip, and tiny babies help it surprise everyone.
Mother weighs this much more than her newborn
key: Mother weighs this much more than her newborn
why: About 99% bamboo, about 12 kg a day, a newborn about 1/800 of its mother's weight, about 1,900 in the wild and a false thumb. It's the giant panda. The red panda also eats bamboo and has a false thumb, but it's much smaller and isn't a bear.
pearl: Pandas have a carnivore's digestive system, so bamboo passes through fast, which is why they eat so much of it. They moved from endangered to vulnerable on the IUCN Red List in 2016.

story: High, huge and slowly going down.

panels.name: Compared with a typical big city

hints: A huge city, high up, built on what used to be a lake.
Sinking about 50 cm a year, and an Olympic host in 1968.
why: About 2,240 m up, sinking almost 50 cm a year in places, about 21.8 million in the greater area, over 300,000 students at UNAM, and built on Lake Texcoco. It's Mexico City, founded as Tenochtitlan. Bogotá is also high up, but it hasn't hosted the Olympics.
pearl: Some parts of the city have sunk by as much as nine metres since the early 1900s. It's the most populous city in North America.

story: End the year on a high.

panels.name: Compared with a typical famous mountain
rows: People who have stood on top

hints: Nothing above sea level gets any taller.
Nepal and China share the summit, and it's about a third of the air pressure at sea level.
why: About 8,849 m high, about a third of sea-level air pressure, winds of about 160 km/h, about −36 °C on a January night, and the Nepal-China border at the top. It's Mount Everest. K2 is the second highest, a very respectable runner-up.
pearl: Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay reached the top on 29 May 1953, and Japan's Junko Tabei became the first woman on the summit in 1975. Happy New Year, from up there.
